provenance: The artist. | With Kanst Gallery, Los Angeles. | | | Exhibited | Oakland, The Oakland Art Museum, Granville Redmond, 3 December 1988 - 29 January 1989. | Laguna Beach, Laguna Art Museum, Granville Redmond, 9 March - 30 April 1989. | Washington D.C., Gallaudet University, Granville Redmond, July 1989. | | Literature | Alma May Cook, 'Paintings on Show at the Galleries,' Los Angeles Evening Express, 24 August 1907, p. 7. | The Oakland Museum, Granville Redmond, Oakland, pp. 56, 96, no. 21, illustrated. | | Granville Redmond was born in Philadelphia and contracted scarlet fever which robbed him of his hearing before his third birthday. Soon after, his parents moved to San Jose, California, and sent him to a specialized school, the California School for the Education of the Deaf and Dumb, and the Blind, Berkeley, California. This was the first school to nurture his love of art and here he would meet two long term advocates Theophilus Hope d'Estrella and Douglas Tilden. | | Redmond went on to study at the San Francisco School of Design. Counted among his early teachers were Arthur Mathews and Amédée Joullin, both of whom often painted in a similar tonalist style. While training as a painter, Redmond became acquainted with many other artists including Gottardo Piazzoni and Giuseppe Cadenasso. Although Redmond was deaf, it did not hamper his relationships with his fellow artists; his lifelong friend Piazzoni even learned sign language. | | Redmond distinguished himself as an art student and won the W.E. Brown medal of excellence. In 1893 he was awarded a grant from the California School of the Deaf which enabled him to study at the Académie Julian in Paris under Jean Paul Laurens and Benjamin Constant. While in Paris, Redmond quickly distinguished himself once again when his large tonalist canvas, "Matin d'Hiver", was accepted for the Paris Salon in 1895. Unfortunately, his success was not sustained and his subsequent submissions to the Salon were rejected. | | Redmond's artistic vision was expanded in France through formal instruction as well as traveling and painting with fellow artists. Faced with financial distress, he moved in with fellow Californian and friend Gottardo Piazzoni in 1897. The two artists much admired the work of the Barbizon painters, particularly Theodore Rousseau. The Californians painted near Fontainebleau some 70 years after the Barbizon artists made the locale so famous. Rousseau's love of trees and the reverential way he painted trees, like a portrait, resonated with the young Californians. They took his philosophy to heart – quoting to each other Rousseau's phrase: "let us make a man breathe, a tree really vegetate." 1 | | With his goal to earn a medal in the Salon thwarted and a significant amount of debt, Redmond returned to California in 1898 and settled in Los Angeles. His old art teacher Theophilus d'Estrella visited Redmond in Los Angeles in 1899 and wrote about the difficulty Redmond was having in advancing his artistic career. Following d'Estrella's criticisms of Los Angeles as an art market, he went on to compliment Redmond: "He has a fine eye for the beautiful even in homely bits of landscape which might escape the eyes of most persons." 2 Redmond found his life partner and married Carrie Robinson in 1899 and in the ensuing few years finally began to find real success in his career. He was selling paintings, and his reputation was growing. In 1902 d'Estrella -ever Redmond's advocate - wrote that "Finally Fortune had begun to smile." And by June of 1905 Redmond was described by d'Estrella as the "foremost artist of Southern California." | | Following an unsuccessful show in 1907 at Steckel gallery, perhaps due in part to the gallery not being of sufficient size for Redmond's larger scale paintings, Redmond moved his work to the Kanst Art Gallery in Los Angeles. Of the painting "California" on offer, in the Los Angeles Express, Saturday, August 24, 1907, Alma May Cook wrote: "Granville Redmond has recently completed his largest landscape painting which he simply calls a California landscape. It is a scene taken in the arroyo near Pasadena, with "Old Baldy" in the distance. In the middle distance a patch of warm sunshine shows the foreground being in half shadow. The painting is hung in the Kanst gallery." | | To the right of center on the horizon, as Alma points out, is the snowcapped peak of Mt. Baldy standing at 10,064 ft., it is the highest point in Los Angeles. For Redmond it is background to the easily missed drama of contrasting tones on display. The trees on view at the center of the horizon provide the chromatic pop that Redmond would later exploit in his depictions of blooming wildflowers. He relies on the less flashy golden yellows, burnt oranges and bright greens of the foliage to provide the contrast with the green and brown grasses and the sandy tones of the arroyo. | | At the center of the painting is the path across the hill. The path is Redmond's only oblique acknowledgement of humankind in the picture. Like his antecedent Rousseau, Redmond found the trees more fascinating than people. Tellingly, the path leads diagonally toward the compositional center of the painting which contains the commanding presence of a single tree overlooking the landscape. Redmond invests this sentinel with an individual and meditative presence. On the left side stands a grove of trees as a subtle counterweight to the power of the tree on the right – like a large family looking with pride on the prodigal child that has struck out to make their way in the world. | | California shows Redmond obsessing over every inch of the massive canvas. There is a detailed and nuanced attention lavished on the sky. A gradual tonal shift takes place from the upper left to upper right corners across the width of the canvas like a gradual echo of the shaded and brightly lit areas in the landscape. The breadth of sky is such that the viewer almost expects the weather to be different from one side of the painting to the other and Redmond does not disappoint. In addition to the tonal changes, the brushwork in the sky is exceptionally varied. The upper right is largely composed of agitated broad blocks of lighter blue interspersed with small contrasting angled dabs of white. The brush strokes gradually decrease in size, contrasting angles and chromatic variance as the landscape meets the sky in the center and along the left side of the painting. On the right edge of the sky, emphasizing the changing weather, the brush strokes are still quite choppy and diverse with the background color quite visible as the spacing is broader as well. This treatment in the sky acts as yet another device to bring the viewer's eyes to the central figure of the tree. | | Redmond's skill as a colorist and his awe at the beauty of California's landscape are on extravagant display in this painting. The artist evokes a sense of quiet through his restrained use of color. This painting, like a Cathedral, encourages soft voices and contemplation. He did not paint out of instinct alone. He enumerated his philosophy, in part, in the Los Angeles Times in 1906: "Artist is colorblind if they pay too much attention to drawing at color's expense." 3. In a 1929 letter Redmond wrote: "Art after all is useful as well as beautiful. One can use it in life as something very tangible. From it I have learned to observe life and nature—a great teacher if one cares to adapt its teachings." 4. Granville Redmond absorbed the lessons and with this masterful work he teaches the rest of us. | | 1.Scott Shields and Mildred Albronda, Granville Redmond: The Eloquent Palette, Portland Oregon, Pomegranate, 2020, p. 43. | 2. ibid p. 4. | 3. ibid p. 51. | 4. ibid p. 35.

provenance: Private collection, Sebastopol, California. | Private collection, Berkeley, California. | Bonhams, Los Angeles, 25 November 2013, lot 43.  | Acquired by the present owner from the above.  |  |  | Beginning in 1903, Arthur Putnam was commissioned by Edward Willis Scripps to produce a series of large outdoor sculptures in bronze for his Miramar Ranch north of San Diego. Putnam did not work on the commission continuously, as he took a lengthy trip to Europe in 1905. Visits to Rome and Paris, as well as a move to San Francisco, delayed the work. But Putnam again took up the commission in 1907. A number of models were made and a handful of full-size figures were cast. Putnam created two life-size puma casts for Mrs. Scripps. The Scripps family bronzes, Puma with Cub and Puma, were cast in 1911 and 1910 respectively. Each is 38 inches tall with a base that measures 20 x 50 inches. These works are still held by the Scripps family. |  | The works in this lot: Puma with Cub and Puma are comparable works and are of identical subject matter. While the bases are of smaller size (17 x 45 inches) the Pumas themselves are of very similar scale. These bronzes have the best elements of Putnam's work: a deft anatomically accurate depiction of the languid but powerful big cats. As Rose Berry wrote in The American Magazine of Art, May 1929, Putnam's work has an impressionistic looseness; he casts aside all haggling detail, leaving in its place something irresistible, something so full of life, movement and the traits and instincts which make life that his work, once seen, is not to be forgotten (p. 280).

Shields, Armin Hansen, The Artful Voyage, Pasadena Museum of California Art, 2015, p. 169, illustrated. | | The son of prominent 19th Century Western artist Herman Wendleborg Hansen, Armin Hansen was an accomplished painter, etcher and draftsman in his own right. Rather than follow in the Western tradition of his father, the younger Hansen's oeuvre largely focuses on maritime scenes marked by rain-soaked decks, turbulent seas, and weathered fishermen. Yet, allusions to the frontier era remain at the forefront of this work with overlapping themes of hard labor taking place beyond the boundary of civilization. The present lot highlights both the physical and mental rigors of seafaring life that are immediately confronted when crossing the safety of the sand bar into the vast unknown of the open sea. | | Hansen first became acquainted with seafaring culture in his early twenties when he was working aboard a trawler in the North Sea off the Belgian Coast. Scenes from this earlier period in his career are much more tonalist in palette, reminiscent of both the Barbizon School and his contemporaries from his native San Francisco, Xavier Martinez and Gottardo Piazzoni. In these earlier works, gray and brown hues make up overcast skies above Belgian port towns like Nieuwpoort and Ostend. Hansen would spend four years working as a deck hand before returning to Northern California where he settled just south of San Francisco in Monterey. Later Monterey works like the present lot use bolder colors. Here deep shades of indigo are broken up by the stark patches of white in the foaming aerated water. Hansen adds intensity of the blues by incorporating dabs of orange to the lone figure and his boat. | | Hansen arrived in Monterey at a time when commercial fishing was beginning to take off. During this next evolution of his style, he brought visibility to the livelihood of Monterey's fisherman while elevating them as worthy of artistic expression. He chose to depict it as it was, reflecting the diversity of its workers, the bustle of a growing commercial fishing port, and modern advancements to the trade. Hansen would often depict close-up views of fisherfolk with strained brows and rolled up sleeves emphasizing the physical toil of the job. While Hansen is best known for his maritime scenes from this period, he does have examples of Western works in his oeuvre (see Salinas Rodeo sold in April 2018 and Cowboy Sport sold in August 2018). In these, cowboys command a horse like a captain commands his ship, each a careful balancing act unsure which way bronco or boat will tilt next. | | The present lot puts less focus on the figure itself and more emphasis on the sea and what lies beyond. With no visible landmarks in the vast scene and only a sliver of sky appearing along the upper edge of the composition, crossing the bar is akin to crossing the frontier – a taxing and isolating endeavor on both the body and the mind. In a poem by Alfred Tennyson of the same name, Crossing the Bar refers to the afterlife or a peaceful transition from safety into the unknown. This perspective of calm amongst the chaos gives the painting a narrative quality wherein the figure has relinquished his fate to the sea. He was particularly fond of the Spanish beach community of Valencia where he met and worked with the Spanish Impressionist Joaquin Sorolla. Sorolla was known to drag large canvases down to the Valencia beaches, tie them down to weather the winds, and paint images on the spot of everyday life along the coast; scenes of fishing boats coming and going, children playing and swimming. Rider, along with other important American impressionist painters, worked side by side with Sorolla painting similar compositions and gleaning as much inspiration from the Spanish master as possible. | | Painted a few years after Sorolla's death, Against the Light is an homage to the Spaniard's influence on Rider and his mastery of Mediterranean light. Here a lone fisherman dons a straw hat to shade himself from the glimmer of the sea as he drags his boat ashore. Light catches the crests of gentle waves and filters through a billowing sail to the point of translucency. In an otherwise cloudless sky, Rider has transformed the sail into a puffy cumulus form. Beyond the shore break, sea and sky blend together with horizontal bands of turquoise and blue. | | Rider went on to exhibit the present lot back home in his native Chicago at the 30th annual exhibition at the Art Institute. Rider continued to be drawn to coastal artist's colonies and ultimately relocated to Laguna Beach in 1931.

Because of his illness, Dixon led a quiet childhood sketching and listening to the tall tales of Native Americans and cowboys told by his paternal grandfather and six uncles. These stories inspired in Dixon a lifelong fascination with the lives of the settlers of the American West, Native Americans and the landscape of the West. | | Dixon's artistic skill was recognized early in his life, however, living in rural California provided little access to formal art instruction. Dixon turned to the engravings in periodicals such as Scribner's and Harper's Weekly to improve his technique. Through these publications, Dixon became familiar with the work of contemporary artists illustrating the American West, chief amongst them Frederic Remington. Remington's dramatic and technical depictions left an indelible impression on young Dixon, and at age 16, Dixon sent two sketch books to Remington for criticism and advice. On September 3, 1891, Remington responded with support, enthusiasm and the instruction to 'draw, draw, draw'. | | Encouraged by Remington's response, Dixon enrolled at the School of Design in San Francisco. He quickly found formal training to be stifling and left before the end of the year. The peripatetic artist spent the ensuing decades building a career as a magazine illustrator--depicting his extensive travel throughout the United States. In the early 1920s Dixon shifted his energy to focus on painting murals. The large surface area of mural painting taught him to distill his painting style into simple but powerful compositions with hard horizon lines and vivid colors. He continued to develop and distill these insights and applied them to his easel paintings. | | Point of Rocks has Dixon's signature clarity of vision. Arthur Millier summarized his abilities writing in 1945: "His technical equipment included fluent, robust draftsmanship, a fine taste in color ... the ability to organize the abstract elements of painting into dramatic and coherent structures. The clear pattern, clearly defined forms and architectural compositions so typical of his pictures reflected the natural choice of the artist's independent mind full as much as the character of the country he painted." 1 | | Maynard Dixon in 1936 possessed the vision and skill to render a simple group of rocks into something monumental and at the same time imbued with an almost human presence. He accomplishes this through palette and line. The intensely saturated blue sky stands as a dramatic background for the focus of the picture which is the Point of Rocks. They are delineated with clean planes via a subdued palette of salmon and sand tones. The structure is the same that Dixon used depicting robed figures. | | 1.Arthur Millier, Maynard Dixon: Painter of the West, Tucson, Arizona, 1945, copyright 1967 by Edith Hamlin.

This painting is included in the catalogue raisonné database Melissa Webster Speidel is compiling of the artist's oil paintings. | | At the height of Frank Tenney Johnson's career as a cowboy-artist, he built a log cabin and studio in Wyoming on Rim Rock Ranch. The land, owned by his cousin Mildred and her husband Earl Martin, was located near the East gate of Yellowstone Park on the North fork of the Shoshone River.1 While Johnson's primary studio and residence at the time remained in Alhambra, California, he would go on to spend almost every summer from 1931 until his untimely death in 1939 painting and hiking around this beloved second home. Painted during the infamous Rim Rock years, A Wyoming Night Herder depicts one of Frank Tenney Johnson's most celebrated subjects, a moment of stillness between a cowboy and his horse set against a starlit night. | | While the Rim Rock years are now synonymous with Johnson's mature career, the artist had a fascination with the American West from an early age. Johnson settled in Wyoming by way of Iowa, where he was born on a humble prairie farm a stone's throw from the historic Overland Trail. Watching the stagecoaches pass by the farm first sparked his imagination and fueled his curiosity about the frontier. By age 14 Johnson and his family had relocated to Milwaukee where visits to the city's first public museum, the Layton Art Gallery, prompted him to become an artist. Johnson went on to apprentice under two German expatriate artists followed by further training at the Art Students League in New York under John Henry Twachtman (1853-1902) and National Academicians Robert Henri (1865-1929) and William Merritt Chase (1849-1916). It wasn't until a 1903 commission with Field & Stream magazine however, that Johnson was finally able to travel extensively throughout the West. On this seminal trip, Johnson visited cattle ranches in Colorado where he observed and developed the heroic cowboy archetype that would become his trademark during the Rim Rock years. | | In A Wyoming Night Herder a cowboy mounted on his Palomino horse pauses for a well-earned cigarette after the day's duties. While the faint glow of the match brightens the figure's face and the rim of his hat, it is moonlight that illuminates the scene. From the figure's crisp white shirt to the metallic on his spurs, the moon shines bright enough to cast shadows on the unmarked trail despite a clouded indigo sky. Seated side-saddle with one leg outstretched and the other hiked up, the figure holds the reins slack in his hands signaling complete trust in his steed. The horse, possibly Tejon, a model Johnson frequently used during this period, gazes into the distance at the rocky outcroppings and the valley beyond. 2 Together the figural vignette represents Johnson's years of experience and observation on the western range revealing a mature style now known as the Rim Rock years. | | 1.Harold McCracken, The Frank Tenney Johnson Book: A Master Painter of The Old West, New York, 1974, p. 123. | 2. ibid, p. 189.
